extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, public-health communicators, encyclopedia editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and documented practices for detecting, countering, and limiting misinformation about COVID-19 across platforms, media, governments, and marketplaces. Covers institutional responses (WHO, publishers, platforms), fact-checking, legal actions, scams, and community editorial policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: WHO infodemic response / myth-busting
rubrics_metrics.description: The World Health Organization described a "massive infodemic" and created a direct WHO 24/7 myth-busting hotline where its communication and social media teams monitor and respond to misinformation through its website and social media pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid, centralized monitoring and timely authoritative rebuttals of false claims (examples debunked by WHO: breath-holding diagnosis, drinking large amounts of water, gargling salt water). Use WHO resources and official materials to correct falsehoods and provide reliable guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform content moderation for harmful misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media companies (Facebook, Twitter, Google) worked with WHO to address misinformation; Facebook stated it would remove content flagged by global health organizations and local authorities that violate its content policy on misinformation leading to 'physical harm'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms should remove or limit content that can cause physical harm and cooperate with health authorities. Examples: Facebook removed millions of posts; but platforms may fail to remove some harmful groups/posts (e.g., groups promoting UV 'therapies' remained). Provide free advertising / promotional support to authoritative health sources when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marketplace enforcement against fraudulent COVID-19 products
rubrics_metrics.description: Online marketplaces (Amazon) removed products that claimed to cure or protect against COVID-19 and removed listings with significant price gouging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marketplaces must detect and delist fraudulent medical products and enforce pricing rules to prevent exploitation. The page notes Amazon removed more than a million products and tens of thousands of overpriced listings, though items sometimes remained on sale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply machine learning and computational detection of fake news
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshops and research were organised for the application of machine learning resources to detect misinformation; researchers monitored the spread of fake news and rumour patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ML tools and interdisciplinary workshops to develop automated detection methods, but be aware of limits and the need for human oversight. The page cites workshops for ML application and researchers tracking rumor propagation across countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase access to authoritative information (open access and lowered paywalls)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many newspapers lowered paywalls for some or all COVID-19 coverage and many scientific publishers made papers related to the outbreak open access (free).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During public-health crises, reducing access barriers to reliable reporting and scientific research improves information availability and counters misinformation. Publishers and media should prioritise open access to authoritative resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain rigorous scientific publishing standards and monitor retractions
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific publishing community must produce quality scholarly publications; infiltration of inferior or false research during COVID-19 led to retractions and raised questions about research reliability. Retraction Watch maintains a database of retracted COVID-19 articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals and publishers should uphold peer review standards and transparent correction/retraction practices. Monitor and document retractions to preserve trust; avoid rushing publication at the cost of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encyclopedic/editorial consensus and reliance on reliable sources (Wikipedia example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wikipedia's coverage and WikiProject Medicine efforts were praised for combating misinformation; from May 2020 the English COVID-19 pandemic page consensus was 'not mention the theory that the virus was accidentally leaked from a laboratory in the article', though this was later debated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encyclopedic and editorial platforms should follow consensus policies, prioritise reliable sources, and avoid introducing fringe or poorly supported hypotheses until sourcing is robust. Collaboration with authoritative organizations (e.g., WHO providing infographics) can improve accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk- and trust-focused public communication strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Research suggests COVID mass media communication should prioritise increasing trust in scientific medicine over attempting to bridge the issue's partisan divide; party and ideology partisanship contributed to lower trust and greater susceptibility to fake news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design public messaging to build confidence in scientific institutions and evidence-based medicine. Recognize partisan dynamics and avoid framing that sacrifices scientific credibility in an attempt to appear neutral across political divides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consumer cybersecurity and scam warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: WHO, FCC, and FTC warned of criminal scams impersonating WHO and other attackers using phishing emails, deceptive domains (e.g., 'cdc-gov.org' vs 'cdc.gov'), and malware sites mimicking trusted resources. Financial scams also exploited stimulus payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise the public to verify official domains, not click suspicious links, not provide personal information, and use official government websites for sensitive submissions. Companies and institutions should post advisories and educate customers about common scam patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government legal responses and censorship risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Many countries enacted 'fake news' laws criminalizing certain types of speech about COVID-19; people were arrested for making posts online. Examples include arrests in Turkey, Iran, Cambodia, Algeria, and many other jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While legal measures may be used to limit harmful disinformation, they carry risks of overreach and censorship. Policymakers should balance public-safety goals with freedom of expression and ensure enforcement is proportionate and transparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of public figures and media in amplifying misinformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Politicians, celebrities, and media outlets (examples: Elon Musk, Donald Trump, Jair Bolsonaro, Joe Rogan, certain radio hosts and news channels) have amplified COVID-19 misinformation, contributing to distrust and harmful behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the outsized effect of influential voices in designing counter-misinformation strategies: engage trusted figures, rapidly correct high-profile falsehoods, and hold public platforms and broadcasters to standards for health-related claims.
